text: 1/5 Pulled out of school in 3rd grade. Here's why.

2/5 In third grade, I got pulled out of in-person school. It wasn't because I was a bad student. It was because the way school was taught didn't fit how I learn. Homeschooling let me work at my own pace and follow ideas I was curious about.
3/5 And it taught me a lot about myself. I ended up graduating high school at thirteen. But finishing early isn't the only point.
4/5 If you're a parent wondering whether this could work for your family, I'll be sharing what worked, what was hard, and what I'd do differently.
5/5 If this was useful, I put together a free 10-question readiness checklist for families. Happy to share it if you'd like.
1/4 School fit everyone the same. I wasn't the same.
2/4 In school, everyone learned the same way, at the same speed. I tried to adapt. It never really fit me. So my family built learning around me. I told my parents what worked and what didn't.
3/4 That's the real power of homeschooling: it can bend to the child.
4/4 If this was useful, I put together a free 10-question readiness checklist for families. Happy to share it if you'd like.
1/4 "But what about socialization?"
2/4 If you're a homeschool parent, you've heard this question. Here's my honest answer. I was homeschooled, and I had just as much social life as other kids, maybe more.
3/4 I was part of local high school clubs and organizations, and I was active in church groups. Socialization didn't happen by accident. It happened because we made room for it.

1/4 Homeschooling at a kitchen table can still feel like school.

2/4 I've seen families start homeschooling and run it just like in-person school. Same linear lessons. Same one-sided teaching. Just at home. But homeschooling can adapt: face to face with an instructor, online with one, or no lectures at all.
3/4 Ask your child what's working and what isn't. Then change it.
4/4 If this was useful, I put together a free 10-question readiness checklist for families. Happy to share it if you'd like.
1/4 I hated my first year of online school.

2/4 I'm going to be honest. My first year of online school, I hated it. At school, the classroom told me where to be and what to do all day. Online, I had lecture times and assignments. And once they were done, I was free. I wasn't used to that.
3/4 If your child is moving from a classroom to online learning, it can feel strange at first. That's normal. I'll share what helped. Free checklist in my bio.

1/3 A homeschool day: 9 to 2

2/3 My school day started at nine. By around two, I was done. The rest of the day was free for other school activities and things I was interested in. That sounds easy. It takes a plan to use it well. Want a simple weekly planner? Link in bio.

1/4 I didn't get to say goodbye.

2/4 I was pulled out of school in the middle of the year. So I didn't get to say goodbye to most of my friends. That was one of the hardest parts. If your child is making this change, talk about the friends they'll miss. Make a plan to stay in touch.
3/4 And know the social side comes back. It took us a while, but it did.

1/4 Freedom isn't a plan
2/4 Online school gave me a lot of free time. I wasn't used to it. At school, the classroom told me where to be. What I needed was an outlook: this time is a gift, so plan something for it.
3/4 If your child is coming from school, talk about the free time before day one. More in my free guide. Link in bio.

1/4 I thought homeschool social life didn't exist.

2/4 In my first year, I honestly thought homeschool social life didn't exist. It did. My parents just didn't know yet what they could sign me up for. It took about a year for them to find local activities and groups.
3/4 After that, I was involved in local high school clubs and organizations and church groups. If you're in that first year and it feels empty, keep looking. It's out there.

1/4 5 places to look for community
2/4 Worried about socialization? Here's where to look. One: clubs and organizations. Local groups often welcome homeschoolers. Check each group's rules. Two: faith and community groups.
3/4 Three: classes and co-ops. Four: volunteering. Five: sports and arts. Pick one this month.

1/4 I told my parents I missed school.

2/4 I told my parents something hard once. I told them I missed being in school. That I felt like I was missing a piece of my childhood. They didn't get defensive. They understood it was a process they were still learning about.
3/4 If your child says something like that, listen first. It's not a failure. It's information.

1/4 How to ask your child for feedback

2/4 Want to know what's working? Ask. Try: what's one thing that works for you? What's one thing that doesn't? Write down the answers. Don't argue. Just listen. Change one thing. Check in again in two weeks.

1/4 Ready or pushed? Here's how to tell.

2/4 Is your child ready, or are they being pushed? From the outside they can look the same. Both are working hard. The difference is what happens when it gets hard. A child who's ready can tell you, and the plan changes.
3/4 A child who's being pushed hides it, and the plan stays the same. Ask them. Then listen.

1/3 Readiness vs. pressure

2/3 Readiness comes from the child's curiosity. Pressure comes from an outside goal, a date or a comparison. When it's hard, a ready child can say so and the plan changes. Protect rest and downtime in both cases. More in the free checklist. Link in bio.

1/4 Signs you might be pushing too fast.

2/4 Here are some signs to watch for. Dread around school. Losing interest in things they love. Cutting out friends to keep up. One sign doesn't mean much. Several together are a signal to slow down and talk. And if you're worried about their well-being,
3/4 please talk to a qualified professional.

1/3 The monthly check-in

2/3 Once a month, sit down together. Ask: what was the best part? What was the hardest? What would you change? Ask: faster, slower, or the same? Write it down. Change one thing. The planner has a check-in page. Link in bio.

1/4 How I started college at 13.

2/4 Here's how I started college at thirteen. I took the PERT test, finished high school, and enrolled. It wasn't hard to get in, because on paper I had everything required. I took most of my classes online, but I still took part in things on campus.
3/4 Rules vary, so check with your college. This is just my path.
4/4 If this was useful, I put together a free 10-question readiness checklist for families. Happy to share it if you'd like.
1/4 Questions to ask a college

2/4 Thinking about college early? Ask these first. What are the age requirements? Which credits transfer? Get it in writing. Who's our contact? What's the withdrawal policy? Are parents involved when the student is a minor?

1/4 Telling my classmates my age.

2/4 There's always a shock moment. When I told classmates how old I was, they were surprised. Because of my path, I matured quickly. That helped me fit in. But it wasn't always easy. If your child is young on campus,
3/4 let them decide how and when to share.

1/3 Start with one class

2/3 You don't have to jump in with a full load. One class is a test of fit. Watch how the workload, the people and the pace feel. Then decide whether to add more. More in the free checklist. Link in bio.

1/4 Finding my footing at FAU.

2/4 After my associate degree at fifteen, FAU felt like a different ballpark. It took some time, but I found my footing. FAU's campus actually had a high school on it, so I made friends with a lot of high schoolers. If your child is making a big jump,
3/4 give them time to adjust.

2/3 At FAU I took in-person classes. It was the first time in years I'd been in a classroom in person. It took adaptation. That's normal. Give yourself time. More in my free checklist. Link in bio.

2/4 Social life in college was a big part of my experience. I was a regular member of clubs and organizations, like Konbit Kreyòl and the Black Student Union. I made a lot of friends there. If your child is young on campus,

1/3 Records you should keep
2/3 Early college means paperwork. Keep transcripts, a course list, your diploma and an activity log. Back it up. Check your state's rules too. A records tracker is in the planner. Link in bio.

1/4 My internship at the state capitol.

2/4 In my second-to-last semester, I did a Florida legislative internship. I spent the legislative session in Tallahassee, working with a state representative. I lived on my own for the first time. It was a new step for me. My age didn't get in the way.
3/4 Homeschooling can lead to things like this.

1/3 Early graduation isn't the only outcome

2/3 People ask: can my child graduate early? Maybe. But it's one door of many. Homeschooling can mean more time for interests, a deeper pace, or a path built around the child. Start with fit, not speed. More in my free checklist. Link in bio.

1/4 Paving the way for my brothers.

2/4 I'm one of three brothers. My other two brothers later followed the same process. So I went in blindly with my parents, and in a way paved the way. If you're the first in your family to try this, it's okay to not know everything yet.
3/4 You learn as you go.

1/4 Pause or continue?

2/4 Not sure whether to speed up or slow down? Ask: does the learner want to continue? Do they understand, not just finish? Are they sleeping, eating and spending time with friends normally? Mostly yes: continue. Mostly no: slow down.

1/4 What I'd tell your family.

2/4 If we were sitting at your kitchen table, here's what I'd tell you. Build learning around your child. Ask for feedback and listen. Change things when they aren't working. And remember: finishing early is one outcome, not the goal.

1/4 Explain it back: a gap check

2/4 Moving fast? Check for gaps. Pick a topic from a few months ago. Ask your child to explain it like they're teaching you. Give a few problems with no hints. If it's shaky, go back before going forward.
